_: China is officially a non-religious state. However, Christmas celebrations are no longer banned, and the secular aspects of Christmas continue to increase in popularity.
December 25 is a public holiday in Pakistan, but is not designated for Christmas, but for the birthday of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan.

Christmas is not a public holiday but is popular despite there being only a small number of Christians. The Japanese have adopted many of the secular aspects of Christmas, such as gift-giving, decorations, and Christmas trees.
Privately celebrated by Armenian and Assyrian communities.
Muslim-majority, though Christian minorities may have small local celebrations.
Muslim-majority. Since the Taliban takeover in 2021 celebrating Christmas has been forbidden, along with many other holidays not part of a narrow Sunni-Islamic perspective.
The religious aspects of Christmas are rarely celebrated, and most secular aspects have been rolled into the New Year's Holiday.
Christmas was banned at one time, but secular aspects of the holiday are appearing with increasing frequency.
Christmas is outlawed since 2016 due to the perception that it is a Western holiday incompatible with the countries' ideology.
In 2025 December 25 was made a public holiday, but as "Constitution Day" rather than Christmas Day.
Christmas has been banned since 2015, when the country adopted Sharia Law.
Even secular aspects of Christmas, such as Christmas trees and gifts, are outlawed in Tajikistan since 2015.
Not an official holiday. However, the Christian community in the country celebrate openly and Baku holds Christmas markets.
Restrictions increased since 2021. Public celebration and decorations banned.
Celebrated by migrant communities. Private home and commercial spaces can put up decorations without fear of punishment.
Comoros is 98% Sunni Muslim. Public celebration is restricted.
